content: Recent updates on North American market conditions from late June 2026 address ongoing container shipping trends, including transpacific spot rate fluctuations and the logistical challenges associated with the peak shipping season [2] . While these insights are vital for understanding the overarching maritime and surface transport environment, they do not specifically address the bulk freight market share nor provide recent historical comparisons for bulk-specific competitors [2] . Additionally, historical analyses, such as discussions from 2022 regarding trade wars and spot rates in the context of 2026 predictions, remain largely speculative and outdated, failing to provide concrete data on market share changes in the years immediately preceding July 2026 [4] . The integration of African and Southeast Asian ports into broader global routing strategies allows operators to mitigate risks associated with over-reliance on single markets while capitalizing on new sources of commodity extraction and industrial consumption. While much of the recent logistical discourse in North America centers on container shipping, specific challenges within the region have profound indirect impacts on the bulk shipping sector. Furthermore, operators navigating North American trade routes must contend with transpacific rate spikes and early peak season challenges that disrupt traditional shipping schedules and capacity planning [12] . Spot rates, fluctuating import volumes, and broader supply chain shifts remain critical metrics for operators attempting to optimize their routing strategies in this highly volatile regional market . The formulation of route strategies and the selection of regional focus areas cannot be decoupled from the broader macroeconomic and geopolitical environment. Broader freight market fluctuations are frequently driven by geopolitical tensions, including the lingering economic effects of previous trade wars and ongoing shifts in international trade alliances [13] . These macro-level variables contribute directly to sudden changes in dry bulk demand and corresponding volatility in freight rates [13] . Freight operators must continuously monitor these geopolitical developments, as they can precipitate the sudden closure of traditional corridors or necessitate the rapid establishment of alternative routes. This volatility has manifested in tangible operational challenges across major trade routes.
